title: pyeCE: A Python Implementation of the Embedded Cluster Expansion
authors: Yann L. Müller, Claire A. Paetsch, Anirudh Raju Natarajan
abstract: The cluster expansion is a widely used approach for predicting the finite-temperature thermodynamics of alloys from zero-kelvin first-principles calculations, but its conventional formulation becomes intractable for materials with more than three or four chemical species. High-entropy alloys have therefore remained largely out of reach. We present pyeCE, an open-source Python library that implements the embedded cluster expansion (eCE), in which machine learning maps many chemical species onto a smaller set of effective species and thereby limits the growth in the number of cluster functions. pyeCE provides the complete modeling workflow, including the construction of symmetry-adapted descriptors with a learnable per-sublattice chemical embedding, a neural-network energy model, ladder-based training, uncertainty quantification, and finite-temperature simulations through Monte Carlo sampling. Built on the PyTorch and pymatgen libraries, it supports systems with multiple species on multiple sublattices and runs on graphics processing units. We demonstrate the package on two material systems. In the first, a single model spanning the full composition space of a 9-component refractory alloy resolves short-range order and order--disorder behavior. This model enables rapid screening for compositions with strong Cr clustering, a feature linked to the formation of a continuous, corrosion-resistant oxide scale. In the second, a model of hydrogen dissolution in a Mo--Nb--W alloy reproduces the composition dependence of hydrogen uptake and resolves the interstitial environments that hydrogen occupies. The modular design of pyeCE allows it to be extended to problems beyond alloy thermodynamics, including kinetics, defect energetics, and the coupling of chemical order to magnetic and vibrational degrees of freedom.
summary: This paper introduces pyeCE, a Python library implementing the embedded cluster expansion (eCE) to overcome the computational limitations of modeling high-entropy alloys. By using machine learning to reduce the complexity of chemical species, it accurately predicts thermodynamic properties like short-range order and hydrogen solubility. This provides a powerful, modular tool for studying complex, disordered materials.
main_problem: Predicting the finite-temperature thermodynamics of complex alloys, especially high-entropy alloys, which are intractable using conventional cluster expansion methods.
main_result: The pyeCE library successfully models short-range order and hydrogen solubility in complex multi-component alloys by employing an embedded cluster expansion formalism.
method: The authors developed an open-source library implementing the embedded cluster expansion (eCE), which uses machine learning to map many chemical species onto a smaller set of effective species.
model_or_system: The model is applied to multi-component alloys (e.g., 9-component refractory alloys, Mo-Nb-W systems) to calculate thermodynamic properties. The eCE uses neural networks trained on DFT data to predict site properties based on symmetry-adapted descriptors.
key_observables: Short-range order, hydrogen uptake ($\langle H/M angle$), local coordination preferences, and total energy.
important_parameters: Temperature (finite-temperature simulations), chemical potentials ($\mu_H$), and the dimensionality reduction factor ($k$).
main_assumptions: The conventional cluster expansion becomes intractable for systems with more than four chemical species, necessitating the eCE embedding approach. Metal atoms are assumed immobile during hydrogen dissolution simulations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the general workflow (eCE construction $ightarrow$ training $ightarrow$ MC sampling), the mathematical steps of the embedding process, and specific results showing how alloy chemistry controls hydrogen solubility and local H-M pair preferences.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the eCE formalism, details the computational workflow (descriptor construction, NN training, MC sampling), and validates the method on two distinct material systems: a 9-component refractory alloy and a hydrogen-dissolving Mo-Nb-W alloy.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter thermodynamics, the use of machine learning (NNs) to parametrize complex many-body interactions and the development of a modular simulation framework are highly relevant to developing advanced Hamiltonians or effective potentials for quantum simulation studies.

figures.caption: FIG. 2. Schematic of the embedded cluster expansion formalism. Given the neighborhood configuration ⃗σi of site i, the site-basis functions φ are projected onto the embedded site-basis functions ˜φ through the learned transformation T . Symmetry-invariant site descriptors ⃗Θ are then computed as in a conventional cluster expan- sion. These descriptors serve as input to a feedforward neural net- work that evaluates the site property xi. The dependence of these quantities on the configuration is suppressed for clarity.

FIG. 1. General workflow of pyeCE. (1) The eCE model is con- structed from the site-basis embedding, the site descriptors, and the site energy model. (2) A training set of symmetrically distinct or- derings is enumerated, evaluated with first-principles calculations, and mapped onto the parent lattice. (3) The model is trained using PyTorch by simultaneously optimizing the transformation matrix T and the site energy model. (4) Finite-temperature properties are predicted by Monte Carlo simulations.

FIG. 3. Illustration of the embedded site-basis functions that map c = 4 species onto k = 3. The four chemical species are represented by four colors (yellow, blue, red, and green). Each species maps to one of four linearly dependent vectors (1, ˜φ1, ˜φ2)T in R3.

FIG. 4. Illustration of the construction of the input matrix η. The example configuration contains 4 atomic sites (1, 2, 3, and 4). The neighborhood of each site consists of the site itself (A) and its 4 near- est neighbors (B, C, D, and E). Element ηij of the input matrix holds the chemical species at neighborhood position j of the ith atomic site.

FIG. 6. Illustration of a site property feedforward neural network. The input layer corresponds to the site descriptors ⃗Θ. The neural network is composed of 2 hidden layers. The final hidden layer pro- duces the latent features ⃗f. The final neuron outputs the site prop- erty xi. The weights w = {w1, w2, w3} and biases in each layer are the trainable parameters.
